sections.heading: ABSTRACT
sections.text: The principle of piezoelectricity has been used to design the micro-electro-mechanical system-based piezoelectric energy harvester for generating electrical energy from the surrounding vibration. The huge popularity of these energy harvesters (EHs) is due to their small size. This paper designs the EH for the heating, ventilation, and air conditioning system. Different cantilever structures with different shapes of the same fabricated area have been designed and investigated at an excited acceleration of $\dot { 1 } \mathfrak { g } ( 9 . 8 \mathsf { m s } ^ { - 2 } )$ ). The multi-perforated cantilever structure has the better stress distribution within the cantilever structure and generates better output voltage and power than their basic design. The proposed tapered multi-perforated cantilever structure has the least value of the resonant frequency of $9 8 . 5 9 \mathsf { H z }$ which is $3 1 . 1 3 \%$ less than the rectangular cantilever structure. The proposed structure generates the output voltage of $\boldsymbol { 1 4 \vee }$ which is $9 1 . 7 8 \%$ higher than the basic rectangular cantilever structure. It also generates the average output power of $7 . 1 5 \mu \mathsf { W }$ which is $2 1 3 . 5 9 \%$ higher than basic rectangular cantilever structure.

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
A recent innovation in the field of the semiconductor devices leads to the development of the small-sized lowpower electronic devices for implanted medical devices [1–3], wireless communication (wireless sensors nodes) [4,5], military equipment, etc. These devices are mostly powered by the conventional battery, which has a lifespan of 6–10 years and needs periodic recharging or replacement. Some of these devices are used in an inaccessible place such as inside the machines or some remote locations or inside the human body such as a pacemaker. The replacement of batteries of these devices becomes difficult. The machine monitoring system is one such system, in which wireless sensor node is placed in an inaccessible place of turbines or an induction motor. So, the devices with the integrated energy harvesting mechanism to recharge the battery are in great demand. The vibration-based energy harvester (EH) is most suitable to power these microdevices [1,4]. Vibration EH utilises the unused vibration energy of the environmental source to generate electrical energy, which are ideal for the low power micro devices. Piezoelectric (PZ) [1,4,5], electrostatic [6] and electromagnetic mechanism [7] are the three different methods to convert surrounding vibration to electric energy. The piezoelectric energy harvester (PZEH) is the most favoured because of its simple design and its ability to produce higher electrical energy. The PZEH does not need any $\circledcirc$ 2021 IETE

external voltage source, as it uses ambient vibration to generate electrical energy. It can easily be implemented using the micro-electro-mechanical system (MEMS) technology [1].

The cantilever-based design is the most widely used in the MEMS-based PZEH as it is easy to fabricate and implement [5,8]. One end of the cantilever beam is fixed, while the other end is free to vibrate. The cantilever beam bends when the load is applied. It returns to the original shape after the removal of load and continues to vibrate due to its inertia and elasticity of the material. The bending of the cantilever structure produces an alternating output voltage. The cantilever beam has the maximum deflection when the resonant frequency of the designed structure $( f _ { p i e z o } )$ is equal to the source frequency $( f _ { s o u r c e } )$ , i.e. $f _ { p i e z o } = f _ { s o u r c e }$ . The cantilever beam in this condition produces maximum output voltage and hence produces maximum output power. The available vibration in our environment is of low frequency [9,10]. There is a considerable success with the MEMS-based EH at low frequency [11,12] in generating considerable voltage and hence can be utilised in different types of application [1,2,13–15]. Initially, researchers focussed on the addition of the proof mass to reduce the resonant frequency [4]. Subsequently, researchers tried to modify the design of cantilever structure to achieve lower resonant frequency [1,2,4,5].

Wireless sensors node which can be used in the dynamic machine monitoring system to monitor the health of the heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HAVC) system. The HAVC system vibrates at twice the line frequency (in India line frequency is $5 0 \mathrm { H z }$ ) which is around $1 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . This battery-operated device requires a continuous power supply to monitor the health of the HAVC system. The integration of EH can easily improve the life span of such devices. However, the challenge is to design the EH with the resonant frequency range of around $1 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ , without increasing fabrication area of the cantilever structure and obtained the sufficient output voltage and power.

There are many research articles [4–6,16] available in the field of PZEHs which is used to power wireless sensor node of machine monitoring system but no such reference was found for HAVC systems as per author’s knowledge. The available vibration is of low frequency in case machine monitoring system, so the main challenge is to design the EH for the low-frequency vibration of very small size. This paper design modelled the EH for the HAVC system with the low resonant frequency and the size of the energy harvester should be within $5 \mathrm { m m }$ .

In this paper, we have proposed multi-perforation in the cantilever structure to improve the performance of the PZEH. The use of multi-perforation not only helps in reducing the resonant frequency but also increases the stress distribution in the cantilever structure. The performance of the proposed designed structure is compared with the rectangular and tapered shaped cantilever structure of the same dimension. The output voltage, power, and stress distribution of each cantilever beams have been obtained. The multi-perforated tapered cantilever beam generates the maximum output voltage at the resonant frequency of $9 8 . 5 9 \mathrm { H z }$ .

The paper is structured as follows. The design parameter and mathematical modelling of the structures are discussed in Section 2. Section 3 discuss the simulation and results of the designed structure. In this section, the design of different PZ cantilever structures have been discussed. This section also discusses the mechanical and electrical analysis involved in the PZ cantilever structure. The comparison of proposed design with available work is carried out in this section. Lastly, the conclusion has been drawn in Section 4.

sections.heading: 2. DESIGN AND ANALYSIS
sections.text:
In this paper, a cantilever beam is designed for the PZEH with the resonant frequency around $1 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ keeping the fabricated length within $5 \mathrm { m m }$ . The modern thin film deposition technique allows as low as $0 . 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ thickness of thin film deposition on the substrate. In this article, PZ layer thickness is $2 \mu \mathrm { m }$ and the silicon substrate layer thickness is $1 3 \mu \mathrm { m }$ which may provide sufficient mechanical strength to support cantilever structure. The Zinc Oxide $( \mathrm { Z n O } )$ layer is sandwiched between the aluminium (Al) electrode. The thickness of the Al electrode is $0 . 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$

In this paper, ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ is used as the PZ material for designing the PZEH. Lead Zirconate Titanate (PZT) has high piezoelectric coefficient $( d _ { 3 1 } = 7 4 1 \ \mathrm { p C / N ) }$ than most of the other known $\mathrm { P Z }$ materials. The presence of Lead in PZT makes it harmful to the environment and is not considered for this study. Some of the biocompatible piezoelectric materials such as $_ { \mathrm { Z n O } }$ [1,2], Aluminium nitride [1,2,17], and Barium Titanate (BaTiO3) [17] are compared along with PZT. The piezoelectric charge coefficient of the $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O } _ { \it \cdot } } }$ , AlN, and $\mathrm { B a T i O } _ { 3 }$ is 11.34, 3.84, and $1 4 9 \mathrm { p C } / \mathrm { N } .$ , respectively [1,2]. The relative permittivity’s of PZT, ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ , AlN, and $\mathrm { B a T i O } _ { 3 }$ are 3400, 12.64, 10.256, and 1200, respectively [1,2]. The ratio of PZ charge coefficient and relative permittivity gives the PZ voltage coefficient. The respective voltage coefficient of PZT, $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O } _ { \it \cdot } } }$ , AlN, and $\mathrm { B a T i O } _ { 3 }$ as calculated are 0.217, 0.897, 0.374, and 0.124 $\mathrm { V m } / \mathrm { N } ,$ respectively [1,2]. ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ has been selected as the PZ materials as it has the maximum voltage coefficient among all the materials discussed here.

sections.text:
The focus of this section is to develop the analytical model of PZ plate cantilever structure. The analytical model has been developed by considering a simple cantilever structure, which has PZ layer on the top of a Si layer. This has been illustrated in Figure 1. The thickness of the PZ layer and substrate layer are $h _ { \mathit { p } }$ and $h _ { s }$ , respectively. In this simplified cantilever structure, the electrode attached to the PZ layer is ignored as the effect of the electrode on the vibration of the cantilever structure is minimal due to its small thickness.

sections.heading: 2.1.2 Mechanical Analysis of the Piezoelectric Plate Cantilever Structure
sections.text:
Researchers gave several techniques to analyse the mechanical vibration of piezoelectric cantilever structures [4,5,13,19–22]. In this article, the thin plate-type cantilever structure with length and width are comparable. The thickness of the cantilever structure is very small as compared to the length and width of cantilever structure. The Kirchhoff plate theory [13,19] has been used to explain the mechanical analysis of the PZ cantilever structure. In this theory, the cross-section of the cantilever structure is perpendicular to the axis of the cantilever structure. Equation (18) shows the transverse displacement of the cantilever plate, as per Kirchhoff plate theory [13,19].

$$

$$

$$

$$

should be zero for the free vibration, i.e. $f ( x , y , t )$ is taken as zero. Equation (19) is modified as Equation (22).

$$
D _ { r } \nabla ^ { 4 } w ( x , y , t ) + \rho h _ { \dot { p } } \frac { \partial ^ { 2 } w ( x , y , t ) } { \partial t ^ { 2 } } = 0
$$

The length and width of a cantilever structure is $L$ and $B _ { ; }$ , respectively. So, the boundaries of the cantilever structure are from $x = 0$ to $L$ and $y = 0$ to $B .$ . The method of separation is used to find the solution of free vibration Equation (22) as,

$$
w ( x , \ y , t ) = W ( x , y ) T ( t )
$$

Substituting Equation (23) in Equation (22) [13,19], we get

$$
\begin{array} { l } { \displaystyle \frac { 1 } { \Gamma ( { \boldsymbol { \mathrm { t } } } ) } \frac { d ^ { 2 } T ( t ) } { d t } = - \omega ^ { 2 } } \\ { \displaystyle \frac { - \beta _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } } { W ( x , y ) } \nabla ^ { 4 } w ( x , y ) = - \omega ^ { 2 } } \end{array}
$$

$\omega ^ { 2 }$ is the constant and $\begin{array} { r } { \beta _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } = \frac { D _ { r } } { \rho h _ { p } } } \end{array}$

Equation (24) and (25) can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle { \frac { d ^ { 2 } T ( t ) } { d t } } + \omega ^ { 2 } \mathrm { T } ( { t } ) = 0 } } \\ { { \nabla ^ { 4 } W ( x , y ) - \lambda ^ { 4 } W ( x , y ) = 0 } } \end{array}
$$

where

$$
\lambda ^ { 4 } = \frac { \omega ^ { 2 } } { \beta _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } } = \frac { \rho h _ { p } \omega ^ { 2 } } { D _ { r } }
$$

For the sinusoidal vibration of the cantilever structure, the general solution of Equation (26) is time dependent as

$$
T ( t ) = A c o s \omega  t + \mathrm { B } \sin \omega t
$$

where A and B are arbitrary constants.

Equation (27) can be solved by expressing the following equation:

$$
( \nabla ^ { 4 } - \lambda ^ { 4 } ) W ( x , y ) = ( \nabla ^ { 2 } + \lambda ^ { 2 } ) ( \nabla ^ { 2 } - \lambda ^ { 2 } ) W ( x , y ) = 0
$$

The complete solution of Equation (30) can be obtained by superimposing the solution of Equations (31) and (32) [19] which are in accordance with the theory of linear

differential equation.

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { ( \nabla ^ { 2 } + \lambda ^ { 2 } ) W _ { 1 } ( x , y ) } } \\ { { \ } } \\ { { \displaystyle \quad = \frac { \partial ^ { 2 } W _ { 1 } ( x , y ) } { \partial x ^ { 2 } } + \frac { \partial ^ { 2 } W _ { 1 } ( x , y ) } { \partial y ^ { 2 } } + \lambda ^ { 2 } W _ { 1 } ( x , y ) = 0 } } \\ { { ( \nabla ^ { 2 } - \lambda ^ { 2 } ) W _ { 2 } ( x , y ) } } \\ { { \ } } \\ { { \displaystyle \quad = \frac { \partial ^ { 2 } W _ { 2 } ( x , y ) } { \partial x ^ { 2 } } + \frac { \partial ^ { 2 } W _ { 2 } ( x , y ) } { \partial y ^ { 2 } } - \lambda ^ { 2 } W _ { 2 } ( x , y ) = 0 } } \end{array}
$$

The solution $W _ { 1 } ( x , y )$ can be represented as the harmonic motion, $W _ { 1 } ( x , y )$ [19] which is written as follows:

$$
W _ { 1 } ( x , y ) = X ( x ) Y ( y )
$$

where

$$
\begin{array} { r } { X ( x ) = c 1 \cos \alpha x + c 2 \sin \alpha x } \\ { Y ( y ) = c 3 \cos \beta y + c 4 \sin \beta y } \end{array}
$$

The product of Equations (34) and (35) will provide the solution of Equation (31) as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { l } { W _ { 1 } ( x , y ) = P 1 \sin \alpha x \sin \beta y + P 2 \sin \alpha x \cos \beta y } \\ { \qquad + P 3 \cos \alpha x \sin \beta y + P 4 \cos \alpha x \sin \beta y } \end{array}
$$

Equation (32) has been solved in similar way as of Equation (31) except iλ. So, the solution of Equation (32) will have the components of product of sinh and cosh terms. Thus, Equation (30) can be rewritten as in Equation (37).

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { W ( x , y ) = P 1 \sin \alpha x \sin \beta y + P 2 \sin \alpha x \cos \beta y } } \\ { { \qquad + P 3 \cos \alpha x \sin \beta y + P 4 \cos \alpha x \sin \beta y } } \\ { { \qquad + P 5 \sinh \theta x \sinh \phi y + P 6 \sinh \theta x \cosh \phi y } } \\ { { \qquad + P 7 \cosh \theta x \sinh \phi y + P 8 \cosh \theta x \cosh \phi y } } \end{array}
$$

where $\lambda = \alpha ^ { 2 } + \beta ^ { 2 } = \theta ^ { 2 } + \phi ^ { 2 }$ and P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P6, P7, P8 are the arbitrary constants whose values will depend on the initial conditions. Equation (28) will give the value of frequency $( \omega )$ as follows:

$$
\omega = \lambda ^ { 2 } \sqrt { \frac { D _ { r } } { \rho h _ { p } } } = \lambda ^ { 2 } \sqrt { \frac { \frac { Y h _ { p } ^ { ~ 3 } } { 1 2 ( 1 - v ^ { 2 } ) } } { \rho h _ { p } } } = \lambda ^ { 2 } \sqrt { \frac { Y h _ { p } ^ { ~ 2 } } { 1 2 \rho ( 1 - \upsilon ^ { 2 } ) } }
$$

where $\lambda$ depend on the boundary conditions of the cantilever structure.

The moment of inertia of the rectangular structure is given by $I = w h _ { p } ^ { 3 } / 1 2 . 5 \mathrm { o }$ , Equation (38) can be rewritten as Equation (39).

$$
\omega = \lambda ^ { 2 } \sqrt { \frac { Y I } { m ( 1 - \upsilon ^ { 2 } ) } }
$$

where $m = \rho w h _ { p }$ is the unit length mass.

The two important observations that can be concluded from the above mathematical analysis are given below.

(i) The voltage generated by piezoelectric plate depends upon the piezoelectric coefficient, applied stress, thickness of the PZ layer and the transverse vibration of the cantilever structure as shown by Equation (11).

(ii) The resonant frequency of a cantilever structures depends on a moment of inertia of a cantilever structure and it may vary with the shape and size of the cantilever structure as shown by Equation (39).

After the mathematical analysis, we will discuss simulation and results of different designed cantilever structures.

sections.heading: 3. SIMULATIONS AND RESULTS
sections.text:
In this section, the model developed in the preceding sections has been verified with the help of the finite element method (FEM) analysis. Different types of cantilever structures have been designed and analysed. The design and the FEM analysis of the cantilever beam are performed in COMSOL Multiphysics 5.3a version. The solid mechanics module and the electrostatics module of COMSOL Multiphysics have been used to analyse the PZ effect in PZ cantilever structures. Normal meshing method is used to mesh the designed cantilever beams. The solid mechanics physics has been used to carry out the mechanical characterisation, whereas electrostatics physics has been used to find the electrical characterisation of the PZ material. The reciprocal of the step size gives the convergence plot of the time-dependent model. The damping coefficient of $0 . 0 0 6 ~ \mathrm { N s / m }$ (or $\mathrm { k g } / { \mathsf { s } } )$ have been used to simulate all the designed cantilever structures at an excitation acceleration of $1 \mathrm { g } ( = 9 . 8 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 } )$ .

First, the rectangular plate cantilever structures have been designed and analysed. Then we designed a tapered cantilever structure and introduced the perforation in the rectangular and tapered cantilever structure and analysed the effect of the modification in the shape of the cantilever structure.

sections.heading: 3.1 Rectangular Plate Structures
sections.text:
The Rectangular cantilever structure is designed according to the Kirchhoff plate theory as discussed in Section 2.1.2 with the resonant frequency of $1 4 3 . 1 6 \mathrm { H z }$ . The different material used in the design of the cantilever structure along with their respective mechanical properties is discussed in subsequent paragraph. The eigen frequency analysis is done in COMSOL multiphysics to find the resonant frequency of the rectangular structure. The variation in the resonant frequency of rectangular structure with proof mass is analysed with the variation in length, width, and thickness of the cantilever structure while keeping other dimensions fixed during the study as shown in Figure 2. When the length of the cantilever structure is increased, there is a decrease in the resonant frequency, whereas resonant frequency gradually increases with the increase in the width and thickness of the cantilever structure as shown in Figure 2.

Since we are designing the energy harvester for HAVC system with the target resonant frequency around $1 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . So, the silicon (Si) based rectangular cantilever structure is designed which has the length equals to $5 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , width is $1 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , and net thickness is $1 6 \mu \mathrm { m }$ as shown in Figure 3. The lowest layer is silicon which has a thickness of $1 3 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The PZ layer is of $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O } _ { \it { 1 } } } }$ , which is sandwiched between two Al electrode layers on the Si layer. The thickness of ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ is 2 and $0 . 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ for the Al layers. The cantilever has the Si-based proof-mass of length $1 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , width $1 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m } .$ , and thickness $8 5 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ This helps in reducing the frequency of designed structure. The resonant frequency of the designed rectangular cantilever structure is $1 4 3 . 1 6 \mathrm { H z }$ .

For appropriate modelling, the different mechanical property of the materials such as modulus of elasticity, density, and Poisson’s ratio, which involved in designing the cantilever structure has been considered. The modulus of elasticity of Si, $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O } _ { \it { 1 } } } }$ , and Al are $1 7 0 \mathrm { G P a }$ [1],

$2 1 0 \mathrm { G P a }$ [1], and $7 0 \mathrm { G P a }$ [23], respectively. The density of Si, $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O } _ { \it { 3 } } } }$ , and Al are $2 3 2 9 \mathrm { k g } / \mathrm { m } ^ { 3 }$ [1], $5 6 8 0 \mathrm { k g } / \mathrm { m } ^ { 3 }$ [1], and $2 7 0 0 ~ \mathrm { k g } / \mathrm { m } ^ { 3 }$ [24], respectively. The Poisson’s ratio of Si, $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O } _ { \it \cdot } } }$ , and Al are 0.29, 0.33 [1], and 0.35 [23], respectively.

sections.heading: 3.2 Structural Modification to Decrease Resonant Frequency
sections.text: Many researchers introduce structural modification on the cantilever structure to decrease the resonant frequency [1,8,10,11,25–33]. Liu et al. [11] designed an Sshaped cantilever structure to attain the low resonant frequency below $3 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . Liu et.al. [31] designed an Si cantilever beam with thin PZT film elements arranged in parallel and Si proof mass to achieve low resonant frequency. In this paper, the low resonant frequency is achieved by reducing the stiffness of the cantilever structure by introducing structural modification and perforation in the cantilever beam.

sections.heading: 3.2.1 Design of Tapered Cantilever Structure
sections.text:
The above mathematical analysis shows (as in Equation (39)) that change in the shape of the cantilever structure can change the resonant frequency. So, in this paper, we have changed the rectangular cantilever structure to the tapered cantilever structure. The tapered cantilever structure is designed in the same fashion as that of the rectangular cantilever structure with Si as the lowest layer. ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ layer is sandwiched between the two aluminium electrodes on the top of the silicon layer. The length of the tapered cantilever structure is $5 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , smaller width is $6 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ and the wider width is $1 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The thickness of the Si layer is $1 3 \mu \mathrm { m }$ and the Al electrode is $0 . 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ and that of the $_ { \mathrm { Z n O } }$ layer is $2 \mu \mathrm { m } .$ , respectively. The proof mass attached at the free end of the tapered cantilever structure is of dimension $1 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m } \times 1 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ $\times ~ 8 5 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The tapered cantilever structure can be fixed at smaller width or at the wider width. The 3D view of both types of tapered cantilever structure is shown in Figure 4(a) and 4(b). The resonant frequency of the tapered cantilever structure fixed at the smaller end is $1 1 7 . 1 7 \mathrm { H z }$ and that of the tapered cantilever structure with wider width fixed has the resonant frequency of $1 7 9 . 2 3 \mathrm { H z }$ . Since we are trying to reduce the resonant frequency of the cantilever structure and the resonant frequency increases in case of the tapered cantilever with wider end fixed. So, the tapered with wider end fixed will not consider in further discussion in this paper. So, throughout the paper, the tapered with smaller width fixed will be known as a tapered cantilever structure.

sections.heading: 3.2.2 Perforation in the Cantilever Structure
sections.text:
The resonant frequency of the cantilever structure can be changed by reducing the spring constant of the cantilever structure which can be achieved either by altering a shape of the cantilever structure or by the use of a proof mass. The change in shape and the proof mass are already introduced in the cantilever structure as discussed in the above section. The increase in the length of the cantilever structure can also decrease the resonant frequency but it will increase the size of the cantilever structure. The decrease in the thickness will compromise the mechanical stability. Hence, the perforation is used in the cantilever design to further decrease the natural frequency without increasing its size. In this paper, two different types of techniques have been used to introduce the perforation. This paper uses the single big perforation and multiple perforations in the cantilever structure and studies the effect of both on the resonant frequency, stress distribution and on the electrical output of the cantilever structure. First, the use of single perforation in the cantilever structure is discussed and later multi-perforation is discussed.

![](images/28aaa9b682593bf671110beb9017b950b4b24b89c5130d899a441ccb26e46a0b.jpg)  
Figure 4: 3D tapered cantilever. (a) Smaller width fixed and (b) wider width fixed

3.2.2.1 Single Perforation in the Cantilever Structure. 3.2.2.1 Single Perforation in the Cantilever Structure.First, we introduce the perforation in the rectangular cantilever structure and tries to reduce the spring constant of the cantilever structure. The length of the perforation used in the rectangular cantilever structure is $1 2 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The width and thickness of the perforation are 500 and $1 6 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , respectively. The perforation starts from $1 3 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ from the fixed end and it is at equidistant from the lateral dimension. The dimension of the proof mass is $1 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m } \times 1 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m } \times 8 5 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The cantilever structure formed after the introduction of perforation is called rectangular perforated cantilever structure and is shown in Figure 5(a). The dimension and distribution of different layers of the rectangular perforated cantilever structure is the same as that of the rectangular cantilever structure. The resonant frequency designed rectangular perforated cantilever structure is $1 2 5 . 2 5 \mathrm { H z }$ , which is reduced from $1 4 3 . 1 6 \mathrm { H z }$ for rectangular cantilever structure. The above dimension of the perforation is selected after the study of its effect on the resonant frequency. The variation of resonant frequency is studied with the variation of length, width and position of the perforation while varying one parameter at a time and keeping all the other parameters constant. Figure 6 shows the variation of resonant frequency with the parameters of perforation.

![](images/54161e70d489598a6ad1bf002370600d3e8c665b0f0fe48284f5bdab43ba673c.jpg)  
Figure 5: (a) 3D Meshed rectangular perforated cantilever and (b) 3D Meshed tapered perforated cantilever

Figure 6 shows that the resonant frequency decreases when there is an increase in the length and width of the perforation but increases with the shift in the position of the perforation away from the fixed end. We discussed the effect of perforation on the rectangular beam which reduces the natural frequency. So, the perforation is used in the tapered cantilever structure in the same way, to further reduce the frequency. Tapered shaped perforation is introduced in the tapered cantilever structure. This brings better mechanical stability in the tapered perforated cantilever beam.

The tapered perforated structure has the same dimension as that of a tapered cantilever structure and it is fixed at the smaller width. The different layer is also the same as that of the tapered cantilever structure. The length of the tapered shaped perforation is $1 2 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ and smaller and wider widths of the tapered shaped perforation are 400 and $5 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , respectively. The perforation starts from $1 3 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ from the fixed end is the same as that of the rectangular perforated cantilever structure. The proof mass is of dimension $1 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m } \times 1 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m } \times 8 5 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The designed cantilever structure is tapered perforated cantilever structure as shown in Figure 5(b) and the resonant frequency is $9 9 . 5 4 \mathrm { H z }$ .

The perfo-3.2.2.2 Multi-perforation in the Cantilever.ration in the cantilever structure not only decreases the resonant frequency but can also use to introduces the discontinuity in the cantilever structure. The discontinuity in the cantilever structure increases stress distribution. The output voltage generated in the cantilever structure is directly proportional to the stress distribution level in the cantilever as discussed in Section 2.1.1. The multiple discontinuities can improve the stress distribution more uniformly in the cantilever structure. The multiple discontinuities can be achieved by introducing multiple perforations in the cantilever beam. The comparison of the stress distribution between all the cantilever is discussed in details in the later section.

First, the effect of the multi-perforation on the rectangular cantilever structure is discussed. The four rectangularshaped perforations are introduced in the rectangular cantilever structure to form a rectangular multiperforated cantilever structure. Each perforation is separated by $5 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The length of each perforation is $2 5 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ and the width is $5 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The first perforation starts at $1 3 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ from the fixed end of the cantilever. The designed cantilever is called a rectangular multiperforated cantilever structure as shown in Figure 7(a). The proof mass is of dimension $1 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m } \ \times \ 1 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ $\times ~ 8 5 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The resonant frequency of the rectangular multi-perforated cantilever structure is $1 2 4 . 3 9 \mathrm { H z }$ .

In the same way, the multiple perforations are introduced in the tapered cantilever structure to form a tapered multi-perforated cantilever structure as shown in Figure 7(b). The four tapered shaped perforations are introduced in the tapered cantilever structure. Each perforation is separated by $5 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The length of each tapered shaped perforation is $2 5 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The smaller width of each tapered shaped perforation is $4 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ and that of the wider width is $5 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The proof mass is of dimension $1 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m } \times 1 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m } \times 8 5 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The resonant frequency of the tapered multi-perforated cantilever structure is $9 8 . 5 9 \mathrm { H z }$ . This helps in achieving the target frequency without increasing the length of a cantilever structure.

The percentage reduction of $2 9 . 3 \%$ is achieved in the resonant frequency of the proposed tapered multiperforated cantilever structure from rectangular cantilever structure.

sections.heading: 3.3 Stress Analysis
sections.text:
The discussion in Section 2.1.1. shows that stress distribution directly affects the amount of the output voltage and power generation capability of the PZ in the cantilever structure. The higher stress is desirable for higher output power and voltage but it should be within the fracture strength of the material. The material loses its elastic property when Von Mises stress in the structure is greater than its Young’s modulus. The maximum Von Mises stress developed in the cantilever beam should be less than modulus of elasticity of the material for proper mechanical stability of the cantilever structure. Figure 8 shows the stress generated by all the structures along the edge of the cantilever structure discussed in this paper at an acceleration of $_ { 1 \mathrm { g } }$ at their respective resonant frequency.

It can be observed from Figure 8 that the stress distribution in the rectangular cantilever structure is higher near the fixed end and gradually decreases when moving away from the fixed end. Same trends can be observed in the case of the tapered cantilever structure. In the above Section 3.2.2, it has been discussed that the perforation not only decreases the resonant frequency but can improve the stress distribution in the cantilever by introducing a discontinuity in the cantilever structure. This can be verified by analysing the stress distribution curve of a rectangular perforated and tapered perforated cantilever structure. There is a sudden jump in the stress level at the start of the perforation, hence distribute stress more uniformly in the cantilever structure. The use of the multi-perforation in case of the rectangular multi-perforated and tapered multiperforated cantilever structures further improves the stress distribution in the cantilever due to multiple points of discontinuity. Hence there are multiple peaks in case of multiperforated cantilever structure. The same trend can be seen in Figure 9 which gives the colour-coded 3D image of the stress distribution in all the cantilever structures. In the case of a cantilever structure with perforation and multi-perforation, stress is higher in the perforation and multi-perforation region than at the fixed end, which is the case in rectangular and tapered cantilever structure. The maximum stress developed in all the cantilever structures is well within the range of the young’s modulus of the materials used in the cantilever as discussed in Section 3.1. Hence the cantilever structure has sufficient mechanical strength and stability.

sections.heading: 3.4.1 Output Voltage
sections.text:
The power and voltage generated by the PZEH device is maximum when the natural frequency of the designed EH is the same as that of surrounding vibration [1,25]. It can be observed from Equation (11) that the PZ layer thickness, voltage coefficient of PZ material and stress distribution within the cantilever structure decides the generated voltage. The sinusoidal output transient voltage is obtained by simulating transient analysis in COMSOL Multiphysics 5.3a. A sinusoidal acceleration of amplitude $_ { 1 \mathrm { g } }$ is applied to all the structures at their respective natural frequency. The transient voltage generated by each cantilever structures is shown in Figure 10 (at their respective resonant frequency).

![](images/1a3eac086c39cc4d286ec4fa685d57300d1e091af1e004b9399ba1c2943428bb.jpg)  
Figure 8: Stress distribution of different cantilever structures along the arc length of edge of cantilever structure

The output voltages produced by rectangular cantilever structure, rectangular perforated cantilever structure, rectangular multiperforated cantilever structure at their respective resonant frequency are 7.3, 11.1 and $1 2 \mathrm { V } ,$ respectively. The output voltages generated by the tapered cantilever structure, tapered perforated cantilever structure and tapered multiperforated cantilever structure are 12, 12.9 and $1 4 \mathrm { V } ,$ respectively, at their resonant frequency. The higher voltage in the perforated and multiperforated cantilever structure than their basic structures is because of the better and higher stress distribution within the structures. Figure 11 shows the value of the output voltage of each of the cantilever structures at a different frequency. The output voltage of each structure is compiled in Table 1.

sections.heading: 3.4.2 Harvested Output Power
sections.text:
Two conditions must be fulfilled in order to extract maximum output power from the PZEH. First, the excitation frequency and resonant frequency should be equal and the second is the impedance matching which means internal resistance $\left( \mathrm { R _ { L } } \right)$ of the PZEH should be equal to the load resistance $( \mathrm { R } _ { \mathrm { P Z } } )$ i.e. $( \mathrm { R _ { L } } ~ = ~ \mathrm { R _ { P Z } } )$ . The equivalent electrical model of the PZEH is shown in Figure 12 in which $\mathrm { V _ { o c } }$ is the open circuit voltage, and Vout is the load voltage (Vout = RL(R R ) $\begin{array} { r } { V _ { o u t } = \frac { R _ { L } } { ( R _ { L } + R _ { P Z } ) } V _ { o c } = \frac { V _ { o c } ^ { } } { 2 } ) } \end{array}$ The output power produced by the PZEH is given by Equation (40). $$ P = { \frac { V _ { o u t } ^ { 2 } } { R _ { L } } } = { \frac { V _ { o c } ^ { 2 } } { 4 * R _ { P Z } } } $$ The value of the internal resistance is required to calculate the maximum power generated by the PZEH. The internal resistance of the PZEH cannot be calculated with any direct method. An external resistance is attached to EH to calculate the internal resistance. The constant load is applied to the PZEH at the fixed resonant frequency. Then the PZ structure is simulated by varying the external resistance to calculate the output power. Figure 13(a) shows the value of the output power at different external resistance. According to the maximum power theorem, the value at which EH produces maximum power will be the optimum load resistance. The value of the load resistance is approximately the same for all the cantilever structures as there is very less variation in the cross-sectional area of the cantilever structure. The value of the optimum load is equal to the internal resistance of PZEH which is approximately 1.6 Mohm for all the structures. ![](images/f902db8af46b6f118f16270ebb41dbb73bdcb2e82648f41134b6687e00a508af.jpg) Figure 9: 3D – stress distribution of all cantilever structures ![](images/8bc55252ae50c0baef99b9d07809f8c71e34e1e9732faeb431c5170802327d32.jpg) Figure 10: Time-dependent output voltages of all cantilevers For each cantilever structure, the output power is evaluated at different vibration frequency which is shown in Figure 13(b). The generated output power of each designed PZ cantilever structure is shown in Table 1. The tapered multiperforated cantilever structure generates an output power of $7 . 1 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { W } ,$ which is $2 1 3 . 5 9 \%$ more than that of the basic rectangular cantilever structure. Lastly, the proposed structures have been compared with the existing works in Table 2. ![](images/94cc8b76433fe840635df4aa6227198dc41f6fa56ae92c42f1fd6bd847150264.jpg) Figure 11: The generated output voltages of each cantilever structure at different vibration frequency After calculating all the mechanical and electrical parameters of all the cantilever structures, we will discuss in details about the effect of the thickness, damping coefficient and excitation acceleration on the generated output power of the cantilever. This means that the generated output power can be increased by increasing the thickness of the piezoelectric layer but it will also increase the resonant frequency of the structure as discussed in Figure 2 and is in agreement with Equation (38). The higher acceleration will increase the generated power but it may compromise the mechanical strength of the structure due to the increase in the effective stress distribution. The increase in the damping coefficient will restrict the movement and hence decrease the generated output power. It can be observed from the above discussion that the proposed tapered multi-perforated cantilever structure has a lower resonant frequency and has better stress distribution and generates more output voltage than all other cantilever structures.

sections.heading: 4. CONCLUSION
sections.text: In this paper, we discussed the effect of the structural modification of the cantilever structure on the resonant frequency, mechanical and electrical property of the cantilever structure. This paper proposed shows the advantage of introducing the perforation in the cantilever structure. We simulated rectangular, tapered, perforated, and multi-perforated cantilever structures on COMSOL Multiphysics and compared between them. We found that the multi-perforated cantilever structures have better stress distribution within the cantilever structure and generates better output voltage and power than their basic design without increasing the size of the cantilever structure. The tapered multi-perforated cantilever structure has the least value of the resonant frequency and performs best among all the cantilever structures discussed. It has the resonant frequency of $9 8 . 5 9 \mathrm { H z }$ and generates an output voltage of $1 4 \mathrm { V }$ and the average output power is $7 . 1 5 \mu \mathrm { W } .$
